Fast fits and fast starts

Source: vignettes/fast-fits.Rmd
fast-fits.Rmd

xaddivortes() fits the AddiVortes model, a sum of Voronoi tessellations, by a fast point fit in place of Markov chain Monte Carlo. The columns are screened by mutual information with the response, the tessellations are built in turn on the running residual, and each round replaces the share with the smallest Bayes factor by fresh tessellations and refits the rest; a final refit chooses the damping of the cell values by generalised cross-validation. The fit has two uses: a fast point estimate, and the starting state of the exact sampler, which changes where the chains start and not the posterior they target. Both are experimental: they need a build with the core’s experimental feature, and each chunk is skipped in a build without it, so a rendering with no output below is that, not a failure. The table of experimental items gives the install command.

A fast fit

Friedman’s first function, five relevant covariates among ten:

library(thiessen)
set.seed(1)
friedman <- function(n) {
  x <- matrix(runif(10 * n), n, 10)
  f <- 10 * sin(pi * x[, 1] * x[, 2]) + 20 * (x[, 3] - 0.5)^2 +
    10 * x[, 4] + 5 * x[, 5]
  list(x = x, y = f + rnorm(n), f = f)
}
train <- friedman(300)
test <- friedman(300)
fit <- xaddivortes(train$x, train$y, seed = 1)
fit
sqrt(mean((predict(fit, test$x) - test$f)^2))

xaddivortes_params() holds the five settings and their defaults; the fit time grows linearly with rounds (default 40).

round(sort(fit$fast$column_scores, decreasing = TRUE), 3)

Intervals

sigma(fit) is the root of the training residual sum of squares over the residual degrees of freedom of the final refit. Those degrees of freedom do not count the choice of the cells, so the intervals of predict(fit, interval = "prediction") can cover less than their level:

y_test <- test$f + rnorm(nrow(test$x))
naive <- predict(fit, test$x, interval = "prediction")
mean(y_test >= naive[, "lower"] & y_test <= naive[, "upper"])

A split-conformal interval (Lei and others, 2018) is calibrated without that assumption: fit on one part of the data and widen the prediction by a quantile of the absolute residuals on the other.

half <- sample(nrow(train$x), nrow(train$x) / 2)
proper <- xaddivortes(train$x[half, ], train$y[half], seed = 1)
scores <- abs(train$y[-half] - predict(proper, train$x[-half, ]))
k <- ceiling(0.95 * (length(scores) + 1))
width <- sort(scores)[k]
mean(abs(y_test - predict(proper, test$x)) <= width)

Fast starts

thiessen(start = "fast") starts every chain from its own fast fit, after which the configured burn-in and draws run. A fast start and a warm start from a previous fit (init) cannot be combined.

control <- thiessen_control(
  general_params = general_params(burn_in = 50, draws = 100)
)
started <- thiessen(train$x, train$y, control, seed = 1, chains = 2,
                    start = "fast")
sqrt(mean((predict(started, test$x) - test$f)^2))

The schedule above is short so that the page builds quickly, and the fit warns that the chains may not have converged. A fast start changes where the chains start; the convergence checks apply as they do to a cold start.

References

Lei, J., G’Sell, M., Rinaldo, A., Tibshirani, R. J. and Wasserman, L. (2018). Distribution-free predictive inference for regression. Journal of the American Statistical Association 113(523), 1094-1111.
